title: A syscall is a trap into the kernel.
lede: User code cannot touch devices or other processes’ memory. write, mmap, clone, ioctl enter the kernel via SYSCALL/SVC: privilege bit on, kernel stack, table lookup by number. Linux x86-64: rax = syscall number, rdi rsi rdx r10 r8 r9 = args. Return in rax; negative is -errno.
diagram: Left: user write(fd, buf, n) — SYSCALL, rax=1. Right: kernel copy_from_user, file_ops.write, back. facts: ~50–200 ns local syscall; getpid ~20 ns with vDSO (no trap). Caption: glibc wrappers. strace shows the trace (plate 373).
what: The only legal door user→kernel. Everything else is a library on top. seccomp filters the table.
why: Why ‘user space’ cannot bind :80 without CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE. Why a bad pointer becomes EFAULT, not a kernel crash.
trap: Busy-looping instead of a blocking syscall. Assuming gettimeofday always traps (vDSO). Treating errno as a global across threads — it is per-thread.

title: A process is an address space.
lede: A process is pid + mm (virtual map) + fd table + one or more threads. fork() duplicates the map (CoW, plate 292). execve() replaces the map and starts at _start. Threads (clone CLONE_VM) share mm and fds; each has its own stack and tid.
diagram: 1 kernel task_struct. 2 mm: 0..heap, mmap, stack, kernel half. 3 files_struct: fd 0,1,2. facts: pid 1..2^22 typical; Linux tid ≠ pid for secondary threads. Caption: plate 75 is share vs isolate; this is the struct.
what: Isolation unit = address space. IPC is pipes, sockets, shm — not touching another process’s pointer.
why: Crash of one process does not zero another’s heap. Containers isolate via extra namespaces (plate 372).
trap: Thinking a pointer from process A is valid in B. fork() without exec in a multithreaded process — only the calling thread survives, locks stuck.

title: The scheduler picks the next thread.
lede: On each timer tick (~1–4 ms HZ) or blocking syscall, the CPU’s runqueue picks a TASK_RUNNING thread. Linux CFS: vruntime, red-black tree, not a fixed slice. SCHED_FIFO/RR are realtime: they preempt CFS until they block. Idle = swapper thread.
diagram: Left CFS: lowest vruntime runs; nice +10 ≈ 0.38× weight. Right FIFO: priority 1–99, no timeslice until yield/block. facts: context switch ~1–5 µs + cold cache (plate 80). Caption: you cannot schedule a process; you schedule a thread.
what: Runnable vs sleeping (TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE). Blocking I/O removes you from the rq.
why: Latency vs throughput. A CPU hog starves others until the tick. RT for audio, not for HTTP.
trap: Busy-wait instead of futex/park. SCHED_FIFO at 99 on a production box — it can starve ksoftirqd and lock up the machine.

title: A page is 4 KiB. The TLB caches translations.
lede: Virtual address = VPN + offset. Offset is 12 bits → 4096-byte pages (x86). The page table (4 levels on 48-bit x86-64) maps VPN → PFN + flags (R/W, U/S, NX, dirty). The TLB caches PTEs; a miss walks memory (plate 79).
diagram: facts: 4 KiB page; 2 MiB / 1 GiB huge pages; 48-bit VA canonical; 4-level walk ~4 cache-line refs; TLB L1 D ~64 entries. 2 MiB huge page = 512× fewer PTEs for that range. Caption: munmap and mmap shoot down TLBs (INVLPG / IPI).
what: Paging granularity is 4 KiB unless you opt into THP/hugetlbfs. Internal fragmentation ≤ 4 KiB−1 per mapping.
why: Why malloc of 1 byte still costs a page the first time (plus metadata). Why sparse virtual maps are cheap until you touch them.
trap: Assuming stack/heap grow by bytes. Walking a 64 GiB array with 4 KiB pages: 16M PTEs, TLB thrash — use huge pages or don’t.

title: A page fault is a miss in the map.
lead: A page fault is a miss
lede: Access a VA with no valid PTE → #PF. Kernel: minor fault = already in RAM (CoW, lazy alloc) just install PTE. Major = disk/SSD (demand from file or swap). SIGSEGV if the map does not allow it (NULL, NX on a jump).
diagram: Left minor: first touch of mmap anonymous → zero page, then private page. Right major: file mmap not in page cache → I/O 100 µs–10 ms. facts: Linux /proc/vmstat pgfault vs pgmajfault. Caption: stack growth is a guarded fault, not infinite.
what: Fault handler is the lazy mapper. rss grows on touch, not on mmap.
why: Why startup ‘allocates’ 1 GiB instantly (virtual) then faults in. Why swap kills latency.
trap: mmap 1 TB and thinking RAM is gone. Touching every page at once (memset) as a ‘warmup’ that just caused a stampede of majors.

title: fork copies the map. Writes copy the page.
lede: fork duplicates mm: child’s PTEs point at the same physical pages, marked read-only. First write in either process → fault → copy the page → mark both writable. execve after fork drops the parent’s pages. That is why fork+exec is cheap compared to copying 100 MiB.
diagram: 1 parent rss 80 MiB. 2 fork, rss still ~80 MiB shared. 3 child writes 1 page → +4 KiB. Caption: posix_spawn. vfork is a trap (child runs in parent’s map until exec). posix_spawn is the API.
what: CoW is per page. Shared file mappings (MAP_SHARED) write through, not CoW.
why: Prefork servers (Apache, Redis on Linux) and why a huge parent with dirty heaps makes fork expensive (page-table copy + later CoW).
trap: fork in a multithreaded process (POSIX: undefined for other threads). Relying on vfork. Measuring ‘fork is instant’ on a 32 GiB RSS JVM.

title: mmap maps a file into the address space.
lede: mmap(addr, len, PROT_READ|WRITE, flags, fd, off) installs PTEs backed by the file’s page cache. Load is a page fault (plate 291), not a read() copy. MAP_SHARED: writes are the file. MAP_PRIVATE: CoW. MAP_ANONYMOUS: no file, zeros.
diagram: Left read(): copy file → user buf, 2× RAM for working set. Right mmap: user VA → page cache page. facts: off and addr should be page-aligned. munmap length too. Caption: ELF loader mmap’s the binary.
what: File as memory. msync to flush MAP_SHARED. MAP_POPULATE prefaults.
why: Databases (plate 338), language runtimes, and why a 2 GiB file can be ‘opened’ without a 2 GiB malloc.
trap: SIGBUS on a truncated file. Assuming mmap writes are durable without msync/fdatasync. Mapping with PROT_EXEC from writable tmp (W^X).

title: A file descriptor is an int in a table.
lead: A file descriptor is an int
lede: fd 0/1/2 = stdin/stdout/stderr. Each process has an fd table: small integers → file (offset, flags, inode). dup2(old, 2) redirects stderr. close(fd) frees the slot; the file dies when the last fd and mmap are gone. RLIMIT_NOFILE default often 1024.
diagram: 1 open → smallest free fd. 2 fork copies the table (shared file offset). 3 CLOEXEC so exec does not leak fds. facts: Linux fd 0..; EMFILE at the rlimit. Caption: sockets, pipes, epoll, timers are fds too.
what: The user-space handle is an int. The kernel object is a file. Two fds can share one offset (dup) or not (two opens).
why: Redirection, daemonizing, ‘too many open files.’ Why leaking fds exhausts the table, not the disk.
trap: close(1) then open() — new fd is 1, logs go to a file you opened. Forgetting CLOEXEC and leaking sockets across exec. Assuming fds are unique across processes.

title: The inode is the file. The name is a link.
lede: Directory entry: name → inode number. Inode: type, mode, uid, size, timestamps, block map. nlink counts names. unlink removes a name; the inode and data live until nlink=0 and no fd. Hard link: two names, one inode, same filesystem. Symlink: a path string.
diagram: Left: rm file while process has fd — space frees at close. Right: ln a b; inode nlink=2. facts: ext4 inode ~256 B; max nlink often 65k. Caption: /proc/pid/fd/N is a name for an open inode.
what: Identity is the inode (device+ino). Paths are lookups. rename is atomic on one filesystem.
why: Why deleting a log that is still open does not free disk. Why ‘same file’ is st_dev+st_ino.
trap: Assuming unlink deletes bytes immediately. Crossing devices with rename (EXDEV). Following symlinks in security checks (TOCTOU).

title: A pipe is a kernel ring buffer.
lede: pipe() returns two fds: write end, read end. Bytes sit in a kernel buffer (Linux default 64 KiB, F_SETPIPE_SZ up to /proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size). Full write blocks (or EAGAIN if O_NONBLOCK). Broken read end → write gets SIGPIPE/EPIPE.
diagram: Left: shell a | b — stdout of a is the write fd. Right: buffer 64 KiB; writer faster → blocks. facts: splice/tee move pages without copy. SOCK_STREAM is a different buffer (socket). Caption: plate 5 is the product view; this is the syscall.
what: Unidirectional byte stream in-kernel. Atomic writes ≤ PIPE_BUF (4 KiB POSIX).
why: Unix composition. Backpressure is blocking, not a polite API.
trap: Ignoring SIGPIPE (process dies). Waiting for both ends in one thread (deadlock). Assuming pipe capacity is unlimited.

title: A signal is an async interrupt to a process.
lead: A signal is an async interrupt
lede: kill(pid, SIGTERM) sets a pending bit. At a safe point the kernel jumps to the handler (or default: terminate, core, ignore, stop). Only async-signal-safe functions in a handler (write, _exit — not malloc, printf). syscalls may return EINTR.
diagram: 1 SIGINT default → terminate. 2 sigaction(SIGINT, handler, SA_RESTART). 3 signalfd/epoll to handle in the event loop instead of a handler. facts: SIGKILL/SIGSTOP cannot be caught. Caption: plate 86 graceful shutdown is SIGTERM then drain.
what: Process-directed async events. Mask with pselect/ppoll/signalfd so you do not race.
why: Ctrl-C, timeouts (SIGALRM — prefer timerfd), child death (SIGCHLD).
trap: malloc in a handler (deadlock). Assuming read() never returns EINTR. Using signal() (unreliable semantics) instead of sigaction.

title: An interrupt preempts the CPU, not your if.
lede: A device raises an IRQ line. The CPU jumps to the vector, kernel runs the ISR (top half, short), then softirq/tasklet/workqueue (bottom half). Your userspace if() is not atomic against this — only against other threads if you lock. cli/sti is kernel-only.
diagram: 1 NIC packet → IRQ. 2 ISR acks, queues skb. 3 ksoftirqd / NAPI poll. 4 your recv syscall unblocks. facts: /proc/interrupts counts; irqbalance. Caption: timer interrupt is how preemption happens (plate 289).
what: Hardware event → kernel. Userspace sees it as a completed syscall, a signal, or a futex wake.
why: Why kernel networking does not run in your process. Why ‘disable interrupts’ is not an app locking strategy.
trap: Spinning in userspace ‘until the device sets a flag’ without a syscall. Counting on instruction-level atomicity for I/O registers from user.

title: Blocking I/O sleeps the thread.
lede: read() on an empty socket: thread leaves the runqueue (sleeps) until data or signal. The CPU runs someone else. O_NONBLOCK: return EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK instead. Async: epoll/io_uring so one thread waits on many fds (plate 300).
diagram: Left blocking: 200 threads × 1 conn, each sleeping in read — stack RAM × 200. Right: 1 thread, epoll_wait, 10k fds. facts: default pthread stack 8 MiB reserved (lazy pages). Caption: Node/nginx = nonblocking + event loop (plate 4).
what: Sleep is the cost of simple code. Nonblocking is the cost of state machines. Neither is ‘faster’ without the metric: connections per RAM vs latency.
why: Thread-per-connection vs evented servers. Why a stuck NFS is D-state (uninterruptible).
trap: Blocking in an event-loop thread (janks everyone). 10k threads as a ‘simple’ C10k solution.

title: epoll waits on many fds. select does not scale.
lede: select/poll copy the fd set every wait — O(n) in registered fds. epoll_ctl registers once; epoll_wait returns only ready fds. Level-triggered: still readable → still reported. Edge: report on state change; you must drain. Linux; kqueue on BSD; IOCP on Windows.
diagram: Left select: FD_SETSIZE often 1024. Right epoll: 10k–1M connections, wait O(ready). facts: EPOLLET edge; EPOLLONESHOT. Caption: io_uring can batch syscalls further.
what: Interest list in the kernel. Ready list out. One thread can wait on the set.
why: C10k/C10M. Language event loops wrap this.
trap: Edge-triggered and not reading until EAGAIN — stall forever. Using select with fd 2048. Blocking recv after epoll said readable for 1 byte of a 1 MB message and then blocking on the rest in a hot thread.

title: Each thread has a user stack and a kernel stack.
lead: Each thread has a user stack
lede: User stack: argv, frames, C alloca, default 8 MiB virtual (ulimit -s). Kernel stack: per-thread, 8–16 KiB on Linux, used during syscalls/IRQs — no deep recursion, no large local arrays in kernel. Overflow of user stack → SIGSEGV (guard page).
diagram: facts: user stack grows down; guard page 4 KiB; pthread_attr_setstacksize; kernel stack THREAD_SIZE 16 KiB x86-64. Caption: Go/Rust async move frames to heaps to mill-ions of tasks.
what: Two stacks, two overflow stories. Kernel stack exhaustion is a panic, not a catchable error.
why: Why 100k threads is a virtual-memory problem even if rss is small. Why kernel coding forbids VLAs.
trap: Recursion of depth 1e6 in user code. Creating 1e5 pthreads at 8 MiB each = 800 GiB VA. Putting a 64 KiB buffer on the kernel stack in a module.

title: nice is a hint. SCHED_FIFO is a promise.
lede: nice 0 is default; +19 is lowest CFS weight; -20 needs CAP_SYS_NICE. It still shares the CPU. SCHED_FIFO/RR at rtprio 1–99 run until they block or a higher RT appears — they can starve CFS, IRQs’ soft side, and ssh. chrt, ionice exist too.
diagram: Left: nice +10 batch job. Right: FIFO 50 audio callback 0.5 ms — OK if it blocks; disaster if it spins. facts: /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_runtime_us 950000/s cap so RT cannot eat 100%. Caption: cgroups cpu.max is the container version (plate 306).
what: CFS = weighted fair. RT = priority. Batch = idle. Pick the class, not a magic number.
why: Latency-sensitive vs bulk. Kubernetes cpu shares vs requests.
trap: renice -20 on a production JVM because ‘it’s important.’ RT without the 95% runtime cap. Confusing nice with I/O priority.

title: /proc is the kernel exported as files.
lede: procfs is not disk. cat /proc/meminfo reads kernel structs. /proc/self/status: VmRSS, Threads, NSpid. /proc/net/tcp: sockets. /proc/sys: tunables (many also sysctl). Parsing these is the API for a lot of observability.
diagram: 1 /proc/PID/cmdline, fd/, maps, smaps. 2 /proc/stat load and cpu ticks (USER_HZ 100). 3 /proc/sys/vm/swappiness. Caption: open+read each time; values change. Some files are 0-size and still produce bytes (seq_file).
what: A filesystem interface to kernel state. Namespaces hide others’ pids.
why: htop, ps, containers’ metrics. Why grep /proc is a reasonable debugging move.
trap: Caching /proc/net/tcp for 5 minutes. Parsing loadavg as ‘CPU %’. Writing to /proc/sys without persistence (sysctl.d).

title: Capabilities split root into bits.
lede: euid 0 used to mean every privilege. Linux capabilities: CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind <1024), CAP_SYS_PTRACE, CAP_NET_ADMIN, … File caps (setcap) and ambient caps in containers. Drop what you do not need. root in a user namespace is not host root.
diagram: Left: setuid-root binary. Right: cap_net_bind_service+ep on the binary; euid is your user. facts: ~40 caps; getpcaps; capsh. Caption: ping used to be setuid; now cap_net_raw.
what: Least privilege as a bitmask. Ambient + bounding set in exec. seccomp is the syscall filter on top.
why: Containers, hardened services, ‘why can’t I bind 443.’
trap: CAP_SYS_ADMIN is almost root. Keeping SYS_PTRACE in prod. Assuming non-root cannot be dangerous (user namespaces + confused mounts).

title: CFS tracks vruntime, not a fixed slice.
lede: Completely Fair Scheduler: each task’s vruntime increases as it runs, slower if weight is higher (nice -20). Pick the leftmost (lowest vruntime) in the rb tree. sched_latency_ns (~6–24 ms) is the target period to cycle runnable tasks, not a hard slice.
diagram: Two tasks equal weight: each ~50% over the period. nice +10 vs 0: ~27% / 73%. facts: /proc/sys/kernel/sched_latency_ns; min_granularity_ns. Caption: EEVDF (recent Linux) is a CFS successor with earlier deadlines.
what: Fairness over a window via virtual time. Sleeping tasks don’t accrue; they get a small catch-up (wakeup preemption).
why: Why a tight loop still shares the CPU. Why nice works without a ‘percent CPU’ field.
trap: Tuning slices in app code. Expecting 1 ms fairness with 1000 runnable tasks on 1 core (granularity floors).

title: cgroups cap CPU and RAM. Docker uses them.
lede: control groups v2: a process tree under /sys/fs/cgroup/… with controllers. memory.max = hard RSS+cache cap → OOM-kill in the cgroup, not necessarily the host. cpu.max = quota/period (100ms). io.max, pids.max. Docker/K8s write these.
diagram: 1 slice app.slice. 2 memory.max 512M. 3 cpu.max 20000 100000 = 0.2 CPU. Caption: oom_score_adj still applies inside. stats in memory.current. Nested cgroups in containers.
what: Kernel accounting + limits on a tree of processes. Namespaces isolate names; cgroups isolate resources (plate 372).
why: Why a leaky container dies at 512 MiB. Why ‘CPU request 200m’ is a quota.
trap: memory.limit without swap accounting (old v1). Bursting through cpu.shares thinking it is a cap (shares are relative, max is the cap).

title: Fetch, decode, execute. Then write back.
lede: The CPU: fetch instruction at PC, decode opcode+regs, execute in ALU/LSU, write back registers, PC+=len (or branch). Pipelines overlap stages. A 3 GHz core is 0.33 ns/cycle; many instructions retire 1–4 per cycle when the pipeline is full.
diagram: 1 IF 2 ID 3 EX 4 MEM 5 WB. Stall on cache miss. facts: Intel uops, ROB hundreds of in-flight ops. Caption: you write C; the pipeline sees uops.
what: Instruction cycle + pipeline. Memory ops go through cache (plate 308). Branches may squash the pipeline (plate 319).
why: Why ‘one line of C’ is not one cycle. Why data layout beats micro-optimizing operators.
trap: Counting C statements as cycles. Assuming in-order like a microcontroller on a 2024 server CPU.

title: L1 is ~1 ns. Disk is ~10 ms.
lede: Approximate grown-up numbers (same core, 2020s x86): L1 1 ns / 4 cycles, L2 4 ns, L3 20 ns, RAM 80–120 ns, NVMe 50–150 µs, HDD seek 5–15 ms, US/EU RTT 80–150 ms. 1 ms = 1e6 ns ≈ 3e6 cycles at 3 GHz. A disk seek is millions of instructions.
diagram: facts-5: L1 32–64 KiB/core, ~1 ns; L2 256 KiB–1 MiB, ~4 ns; L3 16–64 MiB shared, ~20 ns; DRAM 100 ns; NVMe 100 µs. Caption: your numbers will differ; the decades between levels will not.
what: A hierarchy of capacity vs latency. Miss a level, pay the next. Sequential RAM is faster than random (prefetch).
why: Every performance discussion. Big O ignores the 100× between L1 and RAM.
trap: Optimizing code before measuring cache misses. Treating SSD like RAM. Network RTT in the same sentence as L1 without a 1e8 gap.

title: A cache line is 64 bytes.
lede: Caches move 64-byte lines (x86; some ARM 64/128). A load of 4 bytes fills 64. Sequential int32 scan: 16 values per miss. Stride 64 bytes: a miss every element. Align hot structs to 64 if you do not want them split.
diagram: Left: struct { int a; … padding to 64; int b; } on two lines → two misses. Right: a and b on one line. facts: clflush; prefetchnta. Caption: false sharing is this plus two cores (plate 311).
what: The transfer unit is the line, not the load size. Write-back: dirty line evicted later.
why: Array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays. Packet headers.
trap: Linked list of 16-byte nodes: a miss per node. Splitting a heavily incremented counter across a line with unrelated data on another core.

title: Spatial is the next line. Temporal is reuse.
lede: Spatial locality: addresses near this one (arrays, sequential scan). Hardware prefetchers detect strides. Temporal: you will touch this line again soon (loops, stacks). Working set ≤ cache ⇒ hits. Random 10 GiB scan ⇒ DRAM or worse.
diagram: Left: for i in 0..n a[i] += 1 — spatial. Right: hashmap of 1e8 keys — temporal if hot keys fit; else miss. Caption: binary search is ~log n cache-unfriendly jumps.
what: Layout and access order vs cache size. Prefetch helps spatial, not pointer chasing.
why: Why sorting a huge array then scanning beats a hash if you only stream once — and why hash wins for point lookups in cache.
trap: Pointer graphs as default data model on the hot path. ‘Random access is O(1)’ ignoring 100 ns DRAM.

title: False sharing is two cores, one line.
lede: Two cores write adjacent fields that sit in the same 64 B line. The line bounces Exclusive↔Modified (MESI) even though the programmers never shared a variable. Symptom: linear slowdown with cores, high cache-coherence traffic, low actual work.
diagram: Left: struct { atomic n[8]; } — 8 counters, one line, 8 cores = disaster. Right: alignas(64) per counter. facts: 64 B pad. perf c2c / mem events. Caption: Go padded structs; Java @Contended.
what: Coherence is per line. False = no software sharing, still hardware sharing.
why: Why a per-core counter array without padding is slower than a mutex at N=8.
trap: Array of atomics of size 4. ‘But they are different variables.’ They are not different lines.

title: Registers are the working set. RAM is far.
lede: x86-64: 16 GPRs (plus xmm/ymm). ARM64: 31. The compiler’s job is to keep live values in registers. Spill to stack when there are too many — stack is L1 if you’re lucky. A function with 40 live ints will spill.
diagram: facts: ~1 cycle reg-reg add; 4 cycles L1; 100 ns RAM; calling convention uses rdi,rsi,… for args (plate 326). Caption: -O2 is mostly register allocation and inlining.
what: The true fastest memory is architectural registers. Everything else is a cache of RAM.
why: Why tiny hot loops beat fancy algorithms on tiny n. Why ABI matters (which regs are caller-saved).
trap: Volatile on every local ‘so the compiler doesn’t optimize’ — forces RAM. Taking addresses of locals (escapes → stack/heap).

title: Little-endian stores the low byte first.
lede: uint32 0x01020304 in memory on x86: 04 03 02 01. Network protocols (TCP/IP) use big-endian (htonl/ntohl). File formats specify one; mixing without conversion is a portability bug, not a style.
diagram: Left LE: addr+0 = 0x04. Right BE: addr+0 = 0x01. facts: x86/ARM (usually) LE; Java DataOutputStream BE; protobuf has its own encoding. Caption: UTF-8 is byte-oriented; no endian for ASCII. UTF-16 needs a BOM or a spec.
what: Byte order of multi-byte integers. One-byte values are immune.
why: Packet parsing, binary files, mmap’d structs between machines.
trap: Casting a packet buffer to uint32_t* on LE and comparing to a BE spec constant. Assuming ARM is BE (it is almost always LE in phones/servers).

title: -1 is all bits set.
lede: Signed integers: -x is ~x+1. 8-bit: -1 = 0xFF, -128 = 0x80. Addition is the same circuit as unsigned; overflow wraps mod 2^n in hardware. C signed overflow is UB (plate 327); unsigned wrap is defined. Java/Go wrap signed too.
diagram: facts: int32 max 2^31-1 = 2147483647; min -2147483648; 2147483647+1 = min in two’s wrap. Caption: sign bit is the high bit. Right-shift of signed may arithmetically keep the sign (implementation-defined in old C).
what: The encoding is two’s complement on every modern CPU you will use. Range is asymmetric: one more negative.
why: Why uint8 255+1=0. Why abs(INT_MIN) cannot fit.
trap: for (uint8 i=0; i<n; i++) with n=256 — infinite if i is uint8. Comparing signed and unsigned (C promotes).

title: float: 1 sign, 8 exp, 23 mantissa.
lede: binary32: 1+8+23. binary64 double: 1+11+52. Value = ± (1.mantissa) × 2^(exp-bias) except subnormals, ±Inf, NaN. 0.1 is not exact. Money: integers of cents (plate 215). Equality of floats is almost always wrong.
diagram: facts: float ~7 decimal digits; double ~16; eps 2^-52; NaN != NaN; (-0.0)==0.0. Caption: fused multiply-add; rounding mode FE_TONEAREST default.
what: Scientific binary fractions + exponents. Integers above 2^53 are not exact in double.
why: Graphics, ML, sim. Why 0.1+0.2 !== 0.3 in JS.
trap: Balances in float. Looping x += 0.1 expecting 10 iterations to land on 1.0. Using NaN as a sentinel and then sorting.

title: HDD seeks ~10 ms. NVMe is ~100 µs.
lede: HDD: mechanical seek+rotation 5–15 ms → ~100 IOPS. SATA SSD: ~100 µs, 10k–100k IOPS. NVMe: 20–100 µs, 100k–1M IOPS. Sequential GB/s on all of them if you stop seeking. RAM 10–50 GB/s, ~10M random ops/s/core if you miss cache.
diagram: facts: HDD 100 IOPS; NVMe 500k IOPS; 4 KiB random vs 1 MiB seq. fsync on HDD is a seek; on NVMe still 10–100 µs. Caption: RAID and queues (iodepth) exist because one thread cannot fill NVMe.
what: IOPS vs bandwidth are different axes. Random 4K vs sequential 1M differ by 100× on HDD, ~5–10× on SSD.
why: Why databases care about fsync (plate 95). Why log-structured merge trees exist.
trap: Benchmarking with /dev/null or page cache (that is RAM). One fsync per row insert.

title: DMA moves bytes without the CPU.
lede: Direct Memory Access: the device writes/reads RAM via the memory controller. CPU sets up a descriptor (addr, len), device transfers, IRQ when done (plate 298). Zero-copy NICs and NVMe work this way. CPU memcpy of 1 GiB wastes cores and cache.
diagram: 1 driver maps buffer (IOMMU). 2 kick doorbell. 3 device DMA. 4 IRQ, NAPI. Caption: bounce buffers if the device cannot reach high mem. IOMMU is the IO TLB.
what: The CPU programs; the device copies. Cache coherence with DMA is a driver problem (snooping or flush).
why: 10–100 GbE, NVMe queues. Why kernel bypass (DPDK) still uses DMA, just from userspace.
trap: memcpy the packet in the app after the NIC already DMAed it into a buffer you could have parsed. Forgetting the buffer must be DMA-capable (aligned, pinned).

title: Local RAM is faster than the other socket.
lede: Two-socket servers: each CPU has its own DIMMs. Remote access +50–100 ns and less bandwidth (QPI/UPI/Infinity Fabric). numactl --cpunodebind --membind. Linux first-touch: a page is allocated on the node that faults it.
diagram: Left: thread on node0, malloc on node1 — remote. Right: bind both. facts: numactl -H; lscpu NUMA nodes. Caption: a 2-socket box is not twice a 1-socket unless you pin.
what: Memory has a location. Threads have a location. Cross traffic is a tax.
why: Databases, JVMs, HPC on dual-socket. Why ‘32 cores’ is not 32 equal cores.
trap: Starting 64 threads unbound on 2 nodes with a shared allocator. Measuring RAM bandwidth with one thread on the far node.

title: A mispredict is ~15 cycles.
lede: The front end guesses the branch so fetch can continue. Correct: ~1 cycle. Wrong: squash ~10–20 cycles of work. Unpredictable branches in a hot loop (50/50 data) cost more than an extra arithmetic. Sorting or bucketing to make branches boring helps.
diagram: Left: if (a[i] > 0) sum++ on random signs — mispredict storm. Right: branchless cmov / bucket. facts: ~15 cycles; 3 GHz → 5 ns. Caption: virtual calls are branches plus icache.
what: Control locality. Predictors love loops and always-true error checks. They hate random data.
why: Parsers, codecs, interpreters. Why a ‘simple’ interpreter is slow.
trap: Micro-optimizing + while ignoring 50/50 branches on gigabyte scans. Exceptions as control flow on the happy path.

title: Unaligned access splits the load.
lede: A 4-byte load at address 2 crosses a 4-byte (and maybe 64 B line) boundary: two loads + merge, or a fault on strict ISAs (classic SPARC, some ARM). x86 allows it and charges you. Packed structs (__attribute__((packed))) create this on purpose.
diagram: Left: packed {u8, u32} — u32 at offset 1. Right: pad 3 bytes, u32 at 4. facts: alignof(double)=8; malloc alignment ≥ 16 on 64-bit glibc. Caption: SIMD wants 16/32-byte align.
what: Natural alignment = size. Padding is the compiler buying cheap loads.
why: ABI, serialization vs in-memory structs, mmap of on-disk packed formats.
trap: Casting a byte buffer to uint64_t* at offset 3. packed + taking addresses of members and passing to APIs that assume align.

title: SIMD is one instruction, N lanes.
lede: Single Instruction Multiple Data: AVX2 ymm = 8× float32 or 32× i8 per instruction. Compilers auto-vectorize simple loops; intrinsics when they don’t. Data must be packed and aligned-ish. Branchy per-element code will not vectorize.
diagram: facts: SSE 16 B; AVX2 32 B; AVX-512 64 B; NEON 16 B. 8-wide f32 add = 8 adds/cycle/port. Caption: strlen/memcpy in libc are SIMD.
what: Wide registers + wide ops. The loop stride becomes 8 or 16. Remainder scalar tail.
why: Codecs, images, parsers (simdjson), ML inner products.
trap: AVX-512 downclocking a whole core. Mixing ABI with/without AVX (state leak). Assuming auto-vec of pointer-chasing loops.

title: UTF-8 is 1–4 bytes. ASCII is unchanged.
lede: A Unicode code point is U+0000..U+10FFFF. UTF-8: 0xxxxxxx for ASCII (1 byte), then 2–4 byte sequences with 10xxxxxx tails. ‘é’ is 2 bytes, ‘€’ 3, many emoji 4. You cannot index the nth character in O(1) without scanning or a side table. C strlen is bytes, not characters.
diagram: Left: café = 63 61 66 c3 a9 (5 bytes, 4 letters). Right: UTF-16 JS: ‘é’.length 1, emoji with VS often 2. Caption: validate UTF-8; overlong encodings are a security bug.
what: Variable-length encoding compatible with ASCII. Random access is by byte, not by grapheme.
why: Every string in a network protocol. Why CHAR(n) in SQL is a mess.
trap: s[i] as the ith letter. Truncating a buffer at max bytes mid-sequence. Treating UTF-8 as Latin-1.
